claims.text: Israel captured Gaza on 6 June 1967; a Military Governorate was set up that month for the West Bank, Gaza, Sinai and the Golan; in 1982, after the Egypt–Israel peace treaty, the Civil Administration took over; the first Gaza settlement was built in 1970 and by 2005 there were 21 settlements with about 9,000 settlers alongside about 1.3 million Palestinians; Filiu: each settler had about 400 times the land and 20 times the water of a Palestinian farmer.

Israel's Central Bureau of Statistics conducted a census of the West Bank and Gaza in summer 1967; its initial findings (3 October 1967) gave the Gaza Strip 356,000 residents, 175,000 of them in refugee camps, and northern Sinai 33,000.

Fedayeen factions, most prominently the PFLP, and civilian civil disobedience opposed the occupation 1967–71; the NYT's James Feron wrote in October 1970 that Gaza was the only area taken in 1967 where attacks continued unabated, most victims being Arabs.

Under Ariel Sharon the IDF expanded a 'pacification' campaign in 1970 and intensified it after the murder of the Aroyo children in January 1971: mass arrests, house demolitions, wide roads for mechanized forces, deportations and a fence around the strip; in summer 1971 about 2,000 homes were demolished and nearly 16,000 people displaced in Rafah camp and other camps, about 2,000 of them sent to El-Arish and hundreds to the West Bank; Sharon told Time in 1989 that the strip stayed quiet for 15 years; Tessler records the fedayeen fragmented and collective punishment used.

Mada Masr, drawing on Sara Roy, writes that the original Allon Plan envisioned moving hundreds of thousands of Palestinians from Gaza to Sinai and the West Bank, that 12,000 relatives of suspected guerrillas were deported to Sinai detention camps, that displaced families were moved in 1972 to Canada Camp on the Egyptian side of the border, and that their return took about 20 years.

claims.text: After 1967 Israel integrated the occupied territories' economy into its own; Moshe Dayan described them as 'a source of factors of production, especially unskilled labor'; between 1967 and 1990, 35–40 percent of the employed Palestinian labor force worked in Israel, mostly in low-paid jobs; in the early 1990s Israel imposed closures and permits.

Yigal Allon proposed two Nahal settlements in central Gaza in 1968; Kfar Darom was re-established in 1970 as the first agricultural village; the Gush Katif bloc numbered 17 settlements with about 8,600 residents before 2005; evacuation began on 15 August 2005, Netzarim was the last on 22 August, and the army withdrew by 12 September 2005.

The Camp David Framework of 17 September 1978 provided for 'transitional arrangements for the West Bank and Gaza for a period not exceeding five years', 'full autonomy to the inhabitants' under a 'self-governing authority' freely elected to replace the military government, and a withdrawal of Israeli armed forces with redeployment to specified security locations.

Article II of the Egypt–Israel Treaty of Peace (26 March 1979) fixed the permanent boundary at the recognized international boundary between Egypt and former Mandate Palestine, 'without prejudice to the issue of the status of the Gaza Strip'.

After Hamas took control in 2007 and the blockade began, Israel barred Gazan workers from 2007 to 2014; limited 'trader permits' resumed in late 2014 and work permits in late 2021; about 18,500 Gazans held permits on the eve of the war and all were revoked on 10 October 2023.
The First Intifada began in the Jabalia camp in December 1987 (Lockman and Beinin).
